title: Common Mistakes & Red Flags
tagline: Most candidates lose points the same handful of ways. Knowing the traps is half of avoiding them.
summary: The recurring pitfalls that sink interviews — and the fixes.

items.detail: Jumping into boxes and databases before agreeing on requirements. Fix: always spend the first few minutes on scope and non-functional requirements.
Asserting 'we need sharding/caching' with no numbers to back it. Fix: do quick back-of-the-envelope math so decisions are justified.
Designing a detailed DB schema before the high-level picture exists. Fix: breadth first (boxes & flows), then depth on the hard part.
Spending 20+ minutes polishing the high-level diagram and never reaching a deep dive. Fix: keep high-level fast; budget the bulk of time for depth.
Designing in your head. Fix: narrate continuously — the interviewer grades and helps based on what you say.
A lone database, a single load balancer, one queue — with no redundancy. Fix: replicate critical components and call out the failure domains.
Designing only the happy path. Fix: proactively ask 'what happens if this node/region/network fails?' and design for it (retries, idempotency, failover).

items.term: Stateful servers behind a load balancer
items.detail: Storing session/user state in app-server memory, breaking horizontal scaling. Fix: keep app servers stateless; push state to a shared cache/DB.
Name-dropping Kafka/Redis/Kubernetes without justifying them. Fix: introduce each component only when a requirement demands it, and say why.
Microservices, multi-region, and event sourcing for a system with 100 users. Fix: match complexity to the actual scale; start simple and scale when numbers demand it.
Doing slow/non-critical work (sending emails, analytics, image processing) inline on the request path. Fix: push it to a queue and process asynchronously.

blocks.title: The two that hurt most
blocks.text: Ignoring failure modes and bluffing about something you don't understand are the fastest ways to lose a senior interview. Both signal you can't be trusted with real systems. Be paranoid about failure; be honest about the edges of your knowledge.

items.detail: Confidently stating something incorrect. Fix: 'I'm not certain, but here's how I'd reason about it.'
Refusing to consider the interviewer's valid pushback. Fix: defend with reasoning, but adapt when they raise a real issue.
Abandoning every choice at the first 'are you sure?'. Fix: a probe isn't always 'you're wrong' — sometimes it's testing conviction. Defend good decisions.
Presenting choices as the only option. Fix: 'I'll use X over Y because we're optimizing for Z' — always frame as a trade-off.
Steamrolling past the interviewer's questions. Fix: treat every question as a signal about what to address next.

sections.title: A self-check you can run mid-interview

items.title: Did I scope before designing?
items.detail: Are functional + non-functional requirements agreed and visible?

items.title: Can I justify each component?
items.detail: For every box, can I point to the requirement/estimate that demands it?

items.title: Where does this fail?
items.detail: Have I named the SPOFs and what happens on node/region/network failure?

items.title: Am I being decisive about trade-offs?
items.detail: Did I make and justify choices, or am I hedging endlessly?

items.title: Am I going deep enough?
items.detail: Have I reached the genuinely hard component, or just drawn obvious boxes?

blocks.text: Running this checklist silently every few minutes keeps you out of every common trap at once. If any answer is 'no', you know exactly what to do next — which is itself the structured, in-control behavior interviewers reward.

cheatsheet: Process traps: designing before clarifying, skipping estimation, diving too deep too early, bad time mgmt, going silent.
Technical red flags: SPOFs, ignoring failure, stateful app servers, buzzword soup, over-engineering, synchronous everything.
Worst two: ignoring failure modes and bluffing — both say 'can't be trusted with real systems'.
Communication traps: bluffing, stubbornness, caving instantly, no trade-off language, ignoring hints.
Keep app servers stateless; push non-critical work to async queues; match complexity to actual scale.
Introduce a component only when a requirement demands it — and say why.
Mid-interview self-check: scoped? justified? where does it fail? decisive on trade-offs? deep enough?

questions.prompt: A candidate proposes microservices, Kafka, a multi-region active-active database, and Kubernetes for a tool with ~1,000 internal users. What's the red flag, and what should they have done?
answer: The red flag is over-engineering: throwing heavyweight, operationally complex infrastructure at a problem that doesn't need it. For ~1,000 internal users the load is trivial — likely a few requests per second — so multi-region active-active (which exists to solve global latency and regional failover at massive scale) and a microservices+Kafka architecture add enormous operational burden, cost, and failure surface for zero benefit. It signals the candidate reaches for buzzwords rather than reasoning about actual requirements, which is itself a trust issue: in real life they'd burn the team's time building and operating complexity nobody needs.

What they should have done: estimate the load first (1,000 users → negligible QPS), then start with the simplest design that meets it — a single well-provisioned service (a modest monolith is fine), one primary database with a replica for availability and backups, and a cache only if reads warrant it. Then explicitly say: 'this easily handles current scale; *if* we grew to millions of users or needed global low latency, here's how I'd evolve it — split out services, add regional replicas, introduce a queue for async work.' That demonstrates the senior instinct: match complexity to scale, keep it simple, and have a justified evolution path rather than premature, unjustified complexity.
keyPoints: Red flag: over-engineering / buzzword-driven design for trivial scale
Estimate first — 1,000 users is negligible QPS
Start simple: one service + primary/replica DB (+ cache if needed)
Describe a justified evolution path for *if* scale grows
followUps: At what signs would you actually decide it's time to split a monolith into services?

questions.prompt: Why is putting user session state in an app server's memory (behind a load balancer) a red flag?
questions.hint: Think about what horizontal scaling and failover require.
answer: Because it makes the app servers stateful, which breaks the two things a load-balanced tier depends on: horizontal scaling and seamless failover. If a user's session lives in one server's memory, then their subsequent requests must always hit that same server (sticky sessions). That undermines load balancing — you can't freely distribute requests across the pool — and if that server crashes or is removed during a deploy, the user's session is gone and they're logged out or lose state. Adding more servers also doesn't cleanly share the load, because each holds state only it knows about.

The fix is to keep app servers stateless: store session/user state in a shared external store — a distributed cache like Redis, or the database — so any server can handle any request. Now you can scale out by simply adding identical, interchangeable servers, route requests to any of them, and lose a server with no user impact (the next request just goes elsewhere and reads the shared state). Statelessness is what makes a tier elastic and resilient, which is why state-in-server-memory is an immediate red flag in a scalable design.
keyPoints: State-in-memory forces sticky sessions → breaks free load distribution
A server crash/deploy loses that user's session
Fix: stateless servers + shared store (Redis/DB) for session state
Statelessness enables elastic horizontal scaling and seamless failover
followUps: Where would you store session state, and how does that choice interact with latency?
